description: A computer science student aiming to steal the MOOOON!
summary: We developed the NASA CLPS Lunar Mission Browser & Landing Site Navigator, an interactive 3D web dashboard that lets users compare candidate lunar landing sites and launch dates. It addresses the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge by computing Sun and Earth positions over the lunar surface, masking them by local terrain, and showing when a site has sunlight for power and a line of sight to Earth for direct-to-Earth communication. Users can explore a real LRO-based 3D globe, browse NASA CLPS missions, and compare up to four sites side by side, with sensitivity controls for launch delays and small site shifts, plus a battery model that estimates whether a lander survives lunar night. This matters because power and communication windows strongly shape lander design, mission safety, and site selection, especially near the lunar South Pole where illumination changes sharply. The tool runs offline in the browser, exports results, and is unofficial and AI-assisted, with limitations disclosed.
details: The NASA CLPS Lunar Mission Browser & Landing Site Navigator is an interactive, browser-based dashboard for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge that helps planners compare landing sites and launch dates by showing when each site has sunlight for power and a line of sight to Earth for direct-to-Earth communication. It combines a 3D lunar globe built from real LRO-derived topography and CLPS mission pins, a searchable CLPS mission browser with terrain-masked Sun and Earth elevation over the 29.5-day synodic cycle, and a side-by-side site comparison tool (up to four presets, CLPS sites, or custom coordinates) with a 3D sky dome, launch-delay and site-shift sensitivity controls, a battery night-survival model, and CSV/JSON export. It runs entirely offline in the browser using React, TypeScript, Vite, Three.js, Tailwind, and Recharts, with astronomy-engine plus our own IAU/IAG Moon orientation, parallax, and horizon-occlusion code, and an optional FastAPI/Python backend; its data comes from NASA SVS and public CLPS information. It is creative in turning terrain-aware illumination and Earth visibility into mission-level trade-offs within one explorable interface, and it was designed with accuracy limits (no atmospheric refraction, approximate terrain masking), offline reliability, performance, and usability in mind. The project is unofficial and not endorsed by NASA, uses no NASA branding, and discloses that its code was AI-assisted (Claude, Gemini, Qoder) and has not been manually verified or checked against JPL Horizons.
